words.etymon: pie-root-swep-sleep (*swep-); Germanic inchoative formation, not an unchanged PIE present
pie-root-swep-sleep (*swep-); slab pie-lex-swepos (*swépos-) is marked uncertain in the lexicon; precise s-stem reconstruction is not required for the root equation

cognate: Norse sǿtr and Latin suauis continue *sweh₂d-u-; sofna and sopor belong to *swep-. Both express sleep as sweet, rather than merely mentioning sweetness and sleep separately.
drift_or_renewal: Norse verbal construction versus Latin adjective plus sleep noun; Homeric support renews the sweetness adjective with γλυκύς/γλυκερός.
shared_syntax: Latin suaui agrees with ablative sopore. I construe Norse sǿtan, masculine accusative singular, with an understood sleep-object (svefn) of sofna: sleep a sweet sleep. The noun is elliptical, not written in this passage; the intervening clause is parenthetical skaldic syntax.
context: Glúmr answers a question about his sleep with a refusal to sleep sweetly until fighting occurs; Lucretius describes limbs bound by sweet sleep. The Menota text and tagging were checked directly. The wider Homeric sleep epithet supports a conventional poetic association across traditions.

near_miss.why_not: The animal name is cognate and both contexts involve ritual, but Norse leads an old ox to Freyr whereas the Vedic men cook a speckled ox. Neither the verb nor the epithet matches; ordinary sacrificial practice is insufficient.

near_miss.lead: Love someone as one’s own eyes
near_miss.why_not: Neither Greek partner has the affection comparison. A Latin corpus search found a closer parallel, recorded separately as a search lead.

near_miss.lead: A sword bites armour / a missile splits armour
near_miss.why_not: Norse bite and Sanskrit bhittvā share *bheid-, and both concern weapons and armour; however the Norse clause denies cutting the armour and describes crushing bones, whereas the Sanskrit missile pierces armour and heart. The weapon-as-biting figure is not expressed by Sanskrit bhid itself; the evidence is too generic to establish inherited phrasing.

Norse konur with vef and Greek γυναῖκες with ὑφαίνουσι supply cognate vocabulary, but in Herodotus the women trade and the men weave. The syntax expressly reverses the assumed association. The Norse context is supernatural weaving with human heads; Greek is ethnographic contrast.
The Homeric personification is formulaic, but neither Norse pivot personifies sleep or says it seizes anyone. Norse simply reports sleeping. Morning vocabulary does not supply the missing verb.

Search of Homer found Il. 11.53–55 and 16.459–460, genuine blood-rain portents. But Norse rigna/blóð and the Greek rain/blood expressions do not here supply an established cognate pair; the assigned Euripides partner concerns interpreting oracles, not blood rain. Motif similarity alone is insufficient. Homeric parallels were recalled and then verified locally.

near_miss.lead: Live a long life; words figuratively killing
near_miss.why_not: The Norse proverb is striking, but the assigned Latin is a recipe for preserving meat, with no long-life or verbal-killing phrase. No cross-branch slab anchor sustains either figure.

near_miss.lead: Sweet food as a partner for sweet sleep
near_miss.why_not: Sanskrit svādu vyañjanam concerns pleasant food; the repeated taste verb is not the sleep root. It is excluded from the Norse–Latin sweet-sleep claim.

near_miss.lead: Pouring blood in a prophetic dream
near_miss.why_not: The Latin haurire is compatible with Norse ausa at root level, but it draws water from poetic springs, while flowers belong to a separate act of plucking. Blóð and flores cannot turn these different constructions into a shared phrase. Homer Il. 16.459 was also checked for blood-pouring; Greek χέω is not the same root as Norse ausa. No claim on motif alone.

near_miss.lead: Tears from eyes as hail or a spring
near_miss.why_not: The Norse hail simile is not repeated by the Armenian partners. Their eyes-as-fountains language explicitly invokes Jeremiah and is Christian biblical quotation. Cognate eye/tear terms describe a natural relation, while the marked images and transmission histories differ.
The apparent Norse sleep word sofnudust is contextually gathered (sǫfnuðust), not fell asleep. This removes the proposed correspondence to Sanskrit suṣvāpa and Latin somnum; lemma error reported.

near_miss.lead: Come at midnight: kiemur, midri nott ~ uenisti media nocte
near_miss.why_not: Three cognate elements and a similar arrival setting make this worth attention. A Latin corpus search confirmed the wording, but the middle-of-night time expression and come are ordinary compositional language. The Norse castle attack and Plautine conjugal complaint lack a distinctive shared figure or pragmatic formula; inheritance of this entire phrase cannot be defended from these occurrences.

Norse contrasts night with day and light with darkness; Serbian addresses night as full of darkness or uses a darkness expression. The night and darkness roots overlap, but the syntax and rhetorical figure do not: the Norse double merism has no Serbian counterpart. The late recorded Serbian evidence adds transmission uncertainty.

near_miss.lead: Pull a bristle from someone’s nose / urge horses with a goad
near_miss.why_not: The repeated Norse idiom is confrontational. Irish brod is a goad and tráig is a shore in a place-name explanation, not an act of pulling. Shared mapped roots do not reproduce the figure or syntactic relation.

near_miss.lead: Weapon splits shield and strikes breast
near_miss.why_not: The close Norse partner is from the same branch and cannot independently satisfy the anchoring rule; the Greek art description and Irish feat catalogue do not repeat the collocation.

near_miss.lead: Naming witnesses / giving a child a name
near_miss.why_not: Norse nefndi vátta is designation of legal witnesses; Homer’s τίθεσθ᾽ ὄνομ᾽ is assigning a newborn’s name. The shared name-root and incidental daughter mention do not yield the same legal or naming formula.

search_lead.cognate: Norse auga (augunum, dative plural definite) and Latin oculus (oculis, ablative plural) continue the eye root *h₃ekʷ-. Unna and amare are not claimed as cognates.
search_lead.argument: Norse ann henni sem augunum í höfði sér compares affection for a woman to attachment to one’s own eyes. Catullus uses one’s eyes as the same personal standard of affection, intensified by plus rather than equality. The comparison is more specific than generic love language, but inheritance remains uncertain because the verb is renewed and Norse is late. The Latin witnesses are outside this slab, so this is a search lead only.

error.correct_reading: Þverá, place-name, genitive singular after til
error.evidence: The destination of the journey is the farm Þverá; automatic mapping to terkʷ- treats the name as ordinary vocabulary.
The combatant whose foot is threatened is Kári, not a common noun corresponding to geu.
The named fighter seizes a spear. Do not use the mapped common-word root geu as phrase evidence.
Kári turns toward the named opponent Bjarni; this is not a lexical bear or wild-beast designation.
The ships belong to Bróðir and his party. Treating the name as the kinship noun brother supplies a spurious lexical match.
The women clear the tables; some carry washing vessels in the following context. This is the indefinite pronoun/adjective, not sumar, summer.

error.correct_reading: thúath (lenited túath), feminine nominative singular after possessive mo
error.evidence: The oath formula invokes the speaker’s people; tli is the OCR confusion of th. The slab’s unknown lemma obscures túath.
The door-keepers close the door. The noun is not the verbs adcomla or conlá supplied by the automatic lemma.

error.correct_reading: safna/safnask, sǫfnuðust: third-person plural preterite middle, gathered
error.evidence: Strong men gather in one place in the historical explanation; this is not sofna, fall asleep. The sleeping partners are an artefact of the lemma.
The surviving stone remains as a memorial. minuyṓs (smaller) belongs to the comparative, not remembrance.

error.correct_reading: поити, go forth; aorist third-person plural, inherited motion verb
error.evidence: The princes march to the city after arranging their forces. The mapping to *peh₃- drink confuses the motion verb with a drinking-related homograph.
ὁράω is a valid dictionary lemma but its present-stem etymon cannot be transferred to εἶδε. Xerxes sees the ships; the aorist belongs to the weid- stem.

note: All 266 bundles read in order in sections; truncated output recovered where needed. One medium-confidence claim, sixteen near-misses, one search lead, sixteen error reports. Searches used permitted Homer and Latin loaders and Menota XML read as text under python3 -I; the default search index was not accessed because it lies outside the permitted paths. Sweet-sleep claim retains the uncertainty of the Latin nominal stem and the Norse ellipsis. Scratch files confined to /tmp/pie-RS015/.
